blocks.body:
"If $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even." "For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that ..." Mathematical statements are built from a small set of words: not, and, or, if ... then, for all, there exists. Logic studies those words on their own, separated from what the statements are about, so that we can tell when a statement is true just because of its shape and when one statement follows from others.

The first half of this page is propositional logic, which handles not, and, or, if-then. The second half adds variables and the quantifiers "for all" and "there exists" (predicate logic), which is what real mathematics needs. The habits learned here, especially negating statements correctly and reading quantifiers in order, are used in every proof you will ever write.

blocks.title: Propositions and connectives
Tautology, contradiction, equivalence
blocks.body:
A formula is a tautology if it is true under every assignment, a contradiction if it is false under every assignment, and satisfiable if it is true under at least one. Two formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are logically equivalent, written $\varphi \equiv \psi$, if they have the same truth value under every assignment; equivalently, $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ is a tautology.

Equivalent formulas say the same thing in different words, so one may always be replaced by the other inside a proof.

blocks.title: Standard equivalences
blocks.body:
For all propositions $p, q, r$:
$$
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q, \qquad 
eg(p \vee q) \equiv 
eg p \wedge 
eg q \quad 	ext{(De Morgan)}$$
$$p 	o q \;\equiv\; 
eg p \vee q \;\equiv\; 
eg q 	o 
eg p \quad 	ext{(contrapositive)}$$
$$
eg(p 	o q) \equiv p \wedge 
eg q, \qquad p \wedge (q \vee r) \equiv (p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r).$$
The converse $q 	o p$ is not equivalent to $p 	o q$.

Each equivalence involves at most three letters, so it can be verified by checking all $2^3 = 8$ assignments. For the contrapositive: $
eg q 	o 
eg p$ is false only when $
eg q$ is true and $
eg p$ is false, that is when $q$ is false and $p$ is true, which is exactly the one row where $p 	o q$ is false. Likewise $
eg p \vee q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. For the converse, the assignment $p = F$, $q = T$ makes $p 	o q$ true and $q 	o p$ false, so they differ.

blocks.title: Every truth table comes from a formula
blocks.body: Any formula in $p, q, r$ defines a truth function: a rule giving T or F for each of the 8 assignments. Since each of the $2^n$ rows can independently be T or F, there are $2^{2^n}$ truth functions of $n$ letters; for $n = 2$ that is 16. Can every one of them be written with the connectives above? Yes, and the proof is constructive.

blocks.title: Disjunctive normal form
blocks.body: Every truth function of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is expressed by a formula that is a disjunction of conjunctions of letters and negated letters. Consequently $\{\neg, \wedge, \vee\}$ is functionally complete, and so is $\{\neg, \wedge\}$.

If the function is never true, use the contradiction $p_1 \wedge 
eg p_1$. Otherwise, for each row where the function is true, form the conjunction that describes exactly that row: include $p_i$ if $p_i$ is T in that row and $
eg p_i$ if it is F. This conjunction is true in that row and false in every other row. The disjunction of these conjunctions is true precisely in the rows where the function is true. Finally, $\vee$ can be removed using De Morgan: $\varphi \vee \psi \equiv 
eg(
eg \varphi \wedge 
eg \psi)$.

blocks.title: Predicates and quantifiers
blocks.body:
A predicate is a statement with variables, such as $P(x)$: "$x^2 > 2$". It becomes a proposition when a value from a chosen domain is substituted, or when the variable is quantified:

- $\forall x\, P(x)$: "for every $x$ in the domain, $P(x)$";
- $\exists x\, P(x)$: "there is at least one $x$ in the domain with $P(x)$".

The domain matters: $\exists x\,(x^2 = 2)$ is true over $\mathbb{R}$ and false over $\mathbb{Q}$. A variable that is quantified is bound; one that is not is free, and a formula with free variables has no truth value until they are given values.

Negation moves through quantifiers by swapping them:
$$\neg \forall x\, P(x) \equiv \exists x\, \neg P(x), \qquad \neg \exists x\, P(x) \equiv \forall x\, \neg P(x).$$
"Not every swan is white" means "some swan is not white", not "no swan is white".

With several quantifiers, order matters. Over the integers, $\forall x\, \exists y\, (y > x)$ says "for each $x$ there is something bigger", which is true: take $y = x+1$. But $\exists y\, \forall x\, (y > x)$ says "some single integer is bigger than every integer", which is false (it would have to be bigger than itself). In $\forall x\, \exists y$, the $y$ may depend on $x$; in $\exists y\, \forall x$ it may not.

blocks.title: Valid arguments
First-order logic, precisely
blocks.body:
University courses make predicate logic exact. A first-order language fixes symbols: variables, connectives, $ orall$, $=$, and some constant, function and relation symbols (for arithmetic: $0$, $S$, $+$, $\cdot$, $<$). Terms and formulas are then defined recursively: variables and constants are terms; $f(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is a term when the $t_i$ are; $R(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ and $t_1 = t_2$ are formulas; and $
eg\varphi$, $(\varphi 	o \psi)$, $ orall x\, \varphi$ are formulas when $\varphi, \psi$ are. (The other connectives and $\exists$ can be defined from these, for instance $\exists x\,\varphi$ as $
eg  orall x\, 
eg \varphi$.) Because the definitions are recursive, facts about all formulas are proved by [[induction]] on how they are built.

A structure $\mathfrak{A}$ for the language is a nonempty domain together with an interpretation of each symbol; a sentence (a formula with no free variables) is then either true or false in $\mathfrak{A}$, written $\mathfrak{A} \models \sigma$ when true. A sentence $\sigma$ is a logical consequence of a set of sentences $\Gamma$, written $\Gamma \models \sigma$, if $\sigma$ is true in every structure in which all of $\Gamma$ is true. This semantic notion is the one that Gödel's [[completeness-theorem]] matches with formal provability.

blocks.title: A tautology by truth table
blocks.body: Show that $\big((p \to q) \wedge (q \to r)\big) \to (p \to r)$ is a tautology.
blocks.solution: The formula can only be false if $p \to r$ is false, which forces $p = T$ and $r = F$, while the hypothesis $(p \to q) \wedge (q \to r)$ is true. With $p = T$, $p \to q$ true forces $q = T$; then $q \to r$ with $r = F$ is false, a contradiction. So no assignment makes the formula false. (Checking all 8 rows of the truth table gives the same result.) This is the hypothetical syllogism.

blocks.title: Knights and knaves
blocks.body: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Resident A says: "At least one of us two is a knave." What are A and B?
blocks.solution:
Let $a$ mean "A is a knight" and $b$ mean "B is a knight". A's statement is $
eg a \vee 
eg b$, and since A is a knight exactly when the statement is true, we need $a \leftrightarrow (
eg a \vee 
eg b)$.

If $a$ were false, the right side $
eg a \vee 
eg b$ would be true, so the biconditional would fail. Hence $a$ is true, and then $
eg a \vee 
eg b$ must be true, which forces $
eg b$. So A is a knight and B is a knave. Checking all four assignments confirms this is the only solution.

blocks.title: Negating a definition
blocks.body: A sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded if $\exists M\, \forall n\, (|a_n| \le M)$. Write the statement "$(a_n)$ is unbounded" without a negation sign in front, and explain why $\forall n\, \exists M\, (|a_n| \le M)$ says something different.
blocks.solution:
Push the negation inward, swapping each quantifier:
$$\neg \exists M\, \forall n\, (|a_n| \le M) \equiv \forall M\, \exists n\, \neg(|a_n| \le M) \equiv \forall M\, \exists n\, (|a_n| > M).$$
In words: whatever bound you propose, some term exceeds it. For $a_n = n$ this holds (given $M$, take $n = \lfloor M \rfloor + 1$, or $n = 0$ if $M < 0$).

The swapped statement $\forall n\, \exists M\, (|a_n| \le M)$ is true for every real sequence: for each $n$ just take $M = |a_n|$. It only says each term is a finite number, because $M$ is allowed to depend on $n$. Boundedness demands a single $M$ for all $n$.

blocks.title: Counting satisfying assignments
blocks.body: Let $$\varphi_n = (p_1 \vee p_2) \wedge (p_2 \vee p_3) \wedge \dots \wedge (p_{n-1} \vee p_n)$$ for $n \ge 2$. How many of the $2^n$ assignments satisfy $\varphi_n$?
blocks.solution:
An assignment satisfies $\varphi_n$ exactly when no two consecutive letters are both false. Let $s_n$ be the number of such T/F strings of length $n$ (with $s_1 = 2$ for a single letter). Split by the last letter. If $p_n = T$, the first $n-1$ letters can be any valid string: $s_{n-1}$ ways. If $p_n = F$, then $p_{n-1}$ must be $T$ and the first $n-2$ letters are any valid string: $s_{n-2}$ ways (for $n = 2$ this is the single string TF, so set $s_0 = 1$). Hence
$$s_n = s_{n-1} + s_{n-2}, \quad s_0 = 1,\ s_1 = 2,$$
giving $s_2 = 3$, $s_3 = 5$, $s_4 = 8$, $s_5 = 13$: these are the Fibonacci numbers, $s_n = F_{n+2}$ with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$. Even this simple-looking formula is satisfied by a fraction of assignments that shrinks like $(1.618/2)^n$.

blocks.body:
- The converse is not the contrapositive: from "if $n$ is divisible by 4 then $n$ is even" you may not conclude "if $n$ is even then $n$ is divisible by 4".
- "Or" in mathematics is inclusive unless "exactly one" is said.
- The negation of "all are" is "not all are" (some are not), not "none are". The negation of $p \to q$ is $p \wedge \neg q$, not $p \to \neg q$.
- Do not swap quantifiers of different kinds; $\forall \exists$ and $\exists \forall$ are different statements.
- "$p$ only if $q$" means $p \to q$; "$p$ unless $q$" means $\neg q \to p$.

These rules are the raw material of [[proof-methods]]: proof by contrapositive uses $p 	o q \equiv 
eg q 	o 
eg p$, and proof by contradiction uses the fact that a statement whose negation implies a contradiction must be true. The set operations of [[sets-relations]] mirror the connectives ($\cup$ for $\vee$, $\cap$ for $\wedge$, complement for $
eg$). Deciding whether a propositional formula is satisfiable (the SAT problem) is the original NP-complete problem, central to [[p-vs-np]]. First-order logic is the setting for the [[completeness-theorem]], which shows that a simple set of proof rules captures every logical consequence, and, via [[computability]], for the [[incompleteness]] theorems.

1. Use a truth table to decide whether $(p \to q) \to r$ and $p \to (q \to r)$ are equivalent.
2. Express $p \leftrightarrow q$ using only $\neg$ and $\wedge$.
3. Negate "for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$", and say in words what the negation means.
4. Over the domain of positive integers, decide which of $\forall x\, \exists y\, (x \mid y)$, $\exists x\, \forall y\, (x \mid y)$ and $\exists y\, \forall x\, (x \mid y)$ are true.
